lesson.title: Red Power: The American Indian Movement and the Fight for Sovereignty
lesson.summary: In 1968, a group of Native activists in Minneapolis founded the American Indian Movement to confront police brutality and poverty in the city, and within a few years the organization was leading a national fight for treaty rights and tribal sovereignty.
lesson.body:
In 1968, Dennis Banks, Clyde Bellecourt, and other Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) activists in Minneapolis, Minnesota founded the American Indian Movement, AIM, initially as a local response to police harassment of Native residents and to demand better housing, jobs, and schools in the city's Native community. Within a few years AIM had grown into a national organization associated with the broader Red Power movement, a term historians use for Native activism of the late 1960s and 1970s that paralleled and drew energy from the African American civil rights movement.

AIM's goals differed in an important way from the goals of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Where the civil rights movement had largely fought for equal treatment and integration under existing law, AIM and allied Native activists argued that tribes were sovereign nations with treaty rights the United States government had repeatedly violated and ignored, going back over a century. That history included the forced removals of the 1830s, most infamously the Trail of Tears, in which the federal government drove tens of thousands of Cherokee and other southeastern peoples from their homelands, killing thousands along the way. AIM's activists saw themselves as demanding that the United States finally honor the treaties it had signed with tribal nations, not simply asking to be included in mainstream American life.

AIM's most dramatic actions came in the early 1970s. In November 1972, AIM organized the Trail of Broken Treaties, a caravan of Native activists that traveled to Washington, D.C. and occupied the Bureau of Indian Affairs headquarters for several days, presenting a twenty point list of demands for renewed treaty negotiations and tribal self determination. The following year, in February 1973, AIM leaders including Russell Means and Dennis Banks led an occupation of Wounded Knee, South Dakota, the site of the 1890 massacre of Lakota men, women, and children by the U.S. Army. The occupiers, working with Oglala Lakota activists on the Pine Ridge Reservation, were protesting corruption in the tribal government and demanding that the federal government reopen treaty negotiations. Wounded Knee developed into a 71 day armed standoff with federal marshals and FBI agents before it ended in May 1973.

The Wounded Knee occupation drew national media attention to issues that had long been ignored, including poverty, treaty violations, and the federal government's power over tribal governments. It also came at real cost. Two Native activists were killed during the standoff, and AIM leaders faced years of federal prosecution and surveillance afterward. Even so, the movement helped push forward a shift in federal policy toward tribal self determination that continued through the 1970s, including new laws recognizing tribes' authority to run their own schools, courts, and social programs. AIM's insistence on treaty rights and sovereignty, rather than simple inclusion, left a lasting mark on how Native nations pursued their relationship with the United States government.
